Title: Rempang Eco-city
Summary: The Singapore government plans to import 3.4GW of clean electricity from Indonesia by 2035 to meet our 6GW target. One of the projects aimed to supply Singapore with solar energy is Rempang "Eco-City," where Sunseap Group is developing a 2.2 GWp floating solar farm on Batam island, evicting 7,500 indigenous residents with violent military force. Beyond direct intimidation, violence, and criminalization, construction will directly damage mangroves and agricultural land, with Rempang Island meeting up to 50% of Batam’s agriculture demand.

Catalyst Marine and Resources (Cambodia)
SG Entities Involved (formerly Private):

Title: Data centers in Johor
Summary:
Singapore-based companies are building data centres in Johor, under the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone. Construction of data centres in villages without prior inform and consent have been affecting residents’ daily living: land clearing, noise, and dangerous levels of dust pollution.

In Feb 2026, residents of Taman Bayu staged a protest, expressing need for greater transparency and concerns about local water and power supply .50 people protested outside a construction site in Johor’s Gelang Patah, Malaysia. They represented 1,000 residents living with “dangerously poor” levels of air quality due to construction dust, unable to carry out day-to-day activities. The protest is the first of its kind in Malaysia, joining the global backlash against the environmental impact of data centres.
Name of Location: Bridge Kidex Sedenak MY06-01, Sedenak, Kampung Baru Sedenak, Kulai, Johor
Non-SG-based Entities Involved (formerly:
- Singapore’s Economic Development Board (for creation of Johor-Singapore SEZ) 
- SIJORI Growth Triangle (Singapore +1 strategy to offload lower skilled labour intensive work to Johor and Riau)

- Japan’s NTT Data Group (not yet started construction)

Other operators building data centres (not directly related to this case, but of note):
- Singapore government-linked company Keppel built a 10 MW data centre in Johor in 2021
-  DayOne International
Scale of profit: S$53 billion in investments approved as of mid-2025 for data centres in Johor
Environmental Impacts:
AI data centre:

Health Impacts: “dangerously poor” levels of air quality due to construction dust, unable to carry out day-to-day activities.

Title: Nickel mining
Summary:
(General) Indonesia is also expected to increase its production capacity for nickel in both mining and refining, cementing itself in the global nickel supply chain; alongside other critical minerals (IEA, n.d.). Nickel is deeply tied into the political economy of Indonesia as it wields significant geopolitical leverage due to the importance of Nickel in the energy transition. In 2022, Indonesia banned the export of Nickel ores (IEA, n.d.) and remains as a crucial industry in Indonesia’s (green) industrial policy (LKYSPP, 2025). While such control over its supply of raw material exports reflects an attitude to strengthen Indonesia’s domestic economy by developing its downstream production capacity, the growth of the Nickel industry is to be supported by Foreign Direct Investment (LKYSPP, 2025). This includes the financial involvement of Singaporean Banks.

(Obi Island, South Halamera Regency, North Maluku, Indonesia) Maluku is one of the key sites for mining in Indonesia. On Obi Island, the key company that is responsible for mining is Harita Nickel (or PT Trimegah Bangun Persada Tbk) since 2010. The ecocide that is happening because of mining activities is well-documented by BAPTHISTA MARIO YOSRYANDI SARA in their article on Inside Indonesia. Envrionemtnal impacts are severe and are deeply intertwined with the social fabric of communities living in that region.
SG Entities Involved (formerly Private): Harita Nickel (PT Trimegah Bangun Persada Tbk)
Scale of profit: IDR29.6 trillion (2025);  increased by 9.9% compared to 2024

Title: Bauxite mining for aluminum
Summary: Foreign companies and investments are buying out land for mining activities, with little to no consultation with local communities and indigenous populations. Local populations are violently displaced through construction encroachment, militarised forces, and environmental damage upturning ecosystems central to their livelihoods, culture, and sense of place. Singapore serves as a strategic hub for these foreign investment companies, which hold shares through Singapore-based subsidiaries. Singapore is additionally a leading investor in Indonesia's mining industry, financing pollution and displacement of local populations.
Country (profit): China, Singapore, Japan, Malaysia, Hong Kong S.A.R.
Name of Location: PT Bintan Alumina Indonesia, Gunung Kijang, Bintan Regency, Riau Islands
SG Entities Involved (formerly Private):
PT Bintan
Global Aluminium International
China's Shandong Nanshan Aluminium
Nanshan Aluminium Singapore Co. Pte. Ltd.
Scale of profit: In 2023, PT BAI's profit after tax was ~USD 185 million.
Communities affected:
seasonally migrating Bajau Laut and the Orang Suku Laut. Some of these communities share kinship ties with the Orang Selat of Singapore.
Effects include loss of income sources, ancestral graves, and their homes

* PT BAI is the major bauxite miner and aluminium producer in the Galang Batang Special Economic Zone (SEZ). The size of operation is 4 million tonne per year alumina facility 
* Global Aluminium International owns 99% of PT BAI in the Galang Batang Special Economic Zone, Bintan
* China's Shandong Nanshan Aluminium holds a 95% stake in Global Aluminium International.

* Even though the standard corporate tax rate in Singapore is 17%, through Singapore global trader program, the tax incentives imply a 5 or 10% tax rate for  Nanshan Aluminium Singapore.

Title: Wilmar (Oil palm) in Indonesia
Summary: Wilmar is the world’s largest processor and merchandiser of palm and lauric (palm kernel) oils and controls over 43% of the global palm oil trade. Multiple reports show they are destroying tropical forests particularly in Indonesia, pushing endangered animals to the brink of extinction. Furthermore, they have been found guilty of serious human rights abuses including land grabs, forced labour and child labour, gender discrimination, as well as exploitative and dangerous working practices that put the health of workers at risk. The abuses identified were not isolated incidents but due to systemic business practices by Wilmar’s subsidiaries and suppliers. Wilmar is headquartered in Singapore and listed on the Singapore stock exchange with a market capitalisation of US$20.92 billion.
Country (place-based): Indonesia, Malaysia, Uganda, Ghana, Liberia, Ivory Coast
Name of Location: Wilmar International Plantation PKS PT.Musi Banyuasin Indah, Batanghari Leko district, Musi Banyuasin Regency, South Sumatra
Communities affected: Indigenous and local communities are evicted off their land. Smallholder farmers are exploited for labour, with serious human rights violations including child labour and slave labour.
Environmental Impacts: Wilmar was named the world's least environmentally friendly company in 2012 due to forest destruction, including deforestation, peat destruction, and habitat fragmentation for endangered wildlife. Wilmar adopted a No Deforestation, No Peat, No Exploitation policy in 2013, but continues to violate these promises including illegal clearing, peat fires, etc. (https://theecologist.org/2015/may/27/deforestation-exploitation-hypocrisy-no-end-wilmars-palm-oil-land-grabs,

Title: Dole (bananas) & deforestation
Summary: Dole-Stanfilco is part of the Singapore-based Dole Asia Holdings of Itochu Corporation since 2013. The Dole-Stanfilco banana plantation in North Cotabato produces mainly Cavendish bananas in a production process encompassing chemical application, land preparation, cultivation, and harvesting. Dole-Stanfilco also operates a plastic plant that supplies the plastics used for bagging of banana fruit bunches in the field and for wrapping and packing the bananas produced. These activities have resulted in the deforestation of indigenous land in Mount Apo Natural Park (MANP) which is a protected area across the regions of Mindanao and Davao, inhabitated by several indigenous Lumad peoples, mainly Manobos, Bagobos, and Klata. An indigineous leader, Bae Merlin Ansabu Celis was ambushed and killed by four suspected men in August 2020.

Title: Carbon offsets or tree-planting restoration projects
Summary: To offset Singapore's high emissions, the government and companies have signed deals for projects like forest conservation and other nature-based solutions. However, many of these have been criticised for lack of transparency and disregard for local communities, and  violating the right to free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) as granted in the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Title: RGE (Pulp giant) headquartered in Singapore
Summary: Royal Golden Eagle (RGE) is one of the world's largest pulp and paper companies, and is headquarted in Singapore. They are credibly linked to the clearance of 5,565 hectares (13,751 acres) of natural forest in Indonesian Borneo between 2020 and 2024, despite the company’s no-deforestation pledge. RGE says the clearing was likely non-compliant. This illegal clearing is not an exception, as RGE’s growing demand for wood fiber continues to pose “one of the single largest threats to Borneo’s remaining rainforests." Beyond threats to biodiversity, forest clearing has been linked to catastrophic floods across Borneo, threatening communities living in the region.

Title: Cross-border solar export
Summary: As part of efforts to meet its nationally determined climate targets, Singapore is aiming to import about 6 GW of low-carbon electricity by 2035. If all the current projects that hold conditional licenses and approvals come into fruition, about 3.4 GW, or over half, of Singapore’s imported clean energy will come from Indonesia’s Riau Islands. However, there has little disclosure about the locations for the planned large-svale solar projects and the environmental and social safeguards in place to ensure a just transition, so that local communities are not being displaced or left with little access to clean energy while Singapore benefits from the solar energy exports.

Title: Gold mining
Summary:
Illegal gold mining is the largest source of mercury emissions in Indonesia, contaminating rivers, fish, crops and communities, with documented health impacts ranging from toxic exposure to malaria spikes. Illegal mining has destroyed forests, farmland and waterways, reducing rice production, worsening floods, and eroding traditional forest-based livelihoods, leaving communities with polluted landscapes and long-term ecological and economic costs as criminal networks adapt faster than regulators.

Singapore is a key hub for the global gold trade, handing 60% of consumer trade of gold that takes place in Asia. Singapore has no mines itself, but the majority of gold extracted from the region is exported to Singapore (for example, 60% of gold mined in Indonesia is sent to Singapore), which is then a key downstream actor in international gold refineries, bullion production plants, storage facilities and jewellery retail. Singapore's role in gold mining echoes many other extractive industries, where Singapore exists as a prominent financial centre and low-tax platform for regional and global elites, with hub functions for global flows of knowledge, corporate value and wealth optimisation, while absolving blame for environmental degradation and land grabs regionally.

In Didipio Mine, killings have been recorded (since 1990s). The country's first FFTA has been approved for another 25 years despite promises for the project to end.

Title: Dumping of plastic waste
Summary: Singapore generates huge amounts of plastic waste (roughly 1.76 billion plastic items per year), and only recycles around 6% locally. The majority of plastic waste is exported to neighbouring countries to be processed. Once exported, there is little transparency around where the waste goes, with much of it found to be dumped illegally in villages and waterways, causing contamination and sanitation issues that directly affect the health of communities.

Title: Pax Silica
Summary: Pax Silica is a planned infrastructure hub in Central Luzon, led by the US but supported by dozens of countries globally. Singapore is one of the primary founders of the Pax Silica initiative and aims to receive data, critical minerals, and AI gains at the cost of livelihoods and the environment in the Philippines. There are ongoing major concerns around displacement from ancestral lands, water and electricity use, climate impacts, dual use and increased militarisation, and loss of livelihoods, as well as increased state violence and US presence in Philippine soil.
